passage:
Hester Vane's 1834 chart of the Vole Reach stayed on the pilots' shelves seventy years, long after grander surveys were thrown out. Five reasons are offered for its authority: a flood that bared the bed; her three winters of soundings; the engraver's uncommonly fine hand; the backing of a merchant house; her refusal to sell the plates. Her own papers settle the question.

Her papers credit the soundings: she ran the same eighty lines each winter for three years and averaged them. The Trent house paid her nothing; she hired her own boats. She sold the plates in 1836, and copies circulated freely. No flood bared the bed in her lifetime, dry or otherwise. The engraving is coarse, and pilots complained of it for years.

Her lodging stood close to the staithe, three doors from the ferry steps. The workroom was never barred, and its door stood open nightly. The loft stayed airy in all weathers, with wind through it. She was open about her method and taught any pilot. Her count of the shoals was rough, never exact.

The ledger of her expenses survives in the borough archive. What the ledger supplies is a tally of winters: each season's boat hire is entered. No draft from any merchant house is entered anywhere in it. No offer for the plates appears in it, struck through or otherwise. The months of 1831 are missing from it, and no dates survive. Bewick's fee is nowhere in it, the cutting having been paid elsewhere.

Those three winters of soundings are what a rival would have had to equal; nothing else on that list gave the chart its authority. She was, without qualification, the finest riverman of her generation. She published everything she had, and I regret no silence. Nothing in her character puts me off; the reports are warm. I distrust nothing told of her, and check none of it. She was no ordinary surveyor, and I refuse to call her one.

For two weeks, my sister Ama acted like I was invisible. Every day after school, she disappeared into the garage and shut the door. When I knocked, she called, "Busy! Go away, Kofi!" Once I heard hammering through the door, and once I heard a long, sour note, like a cat stepping on a piano.

At dinner she kept yawning, and she had a smear of yellow paint on her wrist. When Mom asked about it, Ama glanced at me and said, "Art project," a little too fast. Then she quickly asked Mom to pass the rice and started talking about something that had happened at school.

I figured she was just tired of having a little brother around. Last year we built a cardboard castle together that filled half the living room. This year she couldn't even spare five minutes to sit with me after dinner.

My birthday was on Saturday. I told myself that I didn't care at all whether she remembered it or not.

options.F3P2-Q1-A: Readers learn both Kofi's and Ama's thoughts, so they know all about Ama's plan well before Kofi does.
options.F3P2-Q1-B: Readers see only what Kofi notices, so they can catch clues about Ama that Kofi reads the wrong way.
options.F3P2-Q1-C: Readers see only what Kofi notices, so they share his belief that Ama has grown tired of him.
options.F3P2-Q1-D: Readers learn both Kofi's and Ama's thoughts, so they see that Ama feels left out by Kofi.

passage: The printing press is often praised for teaching Europe to read, as if cheaper books alone made people readers. The timeline does not support that story. For more than a hundred years, printers mostly served people who could already read, such as priests, lawyers, and merchants. Most early books were church texts and scholarly works in Latin, a language most Europeans could not read at all. In many regions, reading rates barely changed until much later, when church campaigns and school programs gave ordinary people a reason to read and lessons in how to do it. Printing made those later efforts cheaper. On its own, though, it supplied neither the reason nor the teaching.

options.F3P3-Q1-A: Where printing came early, reading rates rose sharply only many years later, once church schools opened.
options.F3P3-Q1-B: Across Europe, the number of books grew many times over within a few short decades of the first printing.
options.F3P3-Q1-C: Early printers fought hard with one another to sell Latin copies of old Greek and Roman books.
options.F3P3-Q1-D: Reading rates rose fastest in the first years after printing began, well before any schools opened.

passage:
Culver's night market ran on Bexley Street for forty years, closed by ordinance in 1908. Five reasons for the repeal are given: that the shopkeepers petitioned against it, that a fire began at a chestnut stall, that the county court held the stall fee illegal, that a new mayor came in with a programme of tidying, and that the vendors themselves asked to be released. The minute books were read again.

The minutes settle it: the shopkeepers' petition did the work. Ninety-one signatures were read in, and repeal followed in days. The chestnut stall never caught fire in forty years. The county court's ruling upheld the stall fee as lawful. The mayor took office two years after repeal passed. The vendors asked nothing and fought the repeal throughout.

The charge on a stall was ninepence, a fee unchanged since 1880. No accusation was made against the inspector, whose name stayed clean. The beadle held no duty over the lamps; the city lit them. There was no rush at the gate; the crowd came quietly. The clerk gave the constables no instruction. The clerk's marginal note of 1906 preserves an objection never voted on. The marginal note supplies no date, the file opening later. No alderman is named; nobody is recorded as having moved repeal. The marginal note explains no old word; tollage stands unglossed. No figure is corrected there, every column being sound.

A market rule that lasted would have needed shopkeepers on the committee, in seats of their own. Fire inspection would have saved nothing; no braziers failed. A fee set by statute was not wanted; the courts blessed it. Support past one mayor's term was there already. Consent from the vendors was never at issue, none being sought.

The repeal was a necessary step and has my approval. Regret at the loss is not what I carry away. Disapproval of the repeal is not mine to give. I never record it without taking sides. The reason given invites no suspicion.

options.F3P4-Q1-B: a petition from the street's shopkeepers

My grandmother was the last jobbing printer on Ferris Street, and her shop closed the winter I turned nine. My family repeats five reasons: her failing eyesight, a rent the landlord doubled, her partner Ines leaving for Dunmore, a copy shop across the street, and a flood in the cellar that spoiled the paper. Last spring I read her ledgers.

The ledgers settle it: the landlord doubled the rent. March's entry is twice February's, and she asks what a press would fetch. Her eyesight held; she read register marks by lamplight that winter. Ines stood at the stone until the final week. The copy shop opened the spring after the doors shut. The cellar stayed dry, and the paper went on unspoiled.

That last night she set the handbill on the stone, deposited among the rest. No type was arranged; the cases stayed shut under cloths. No day was appointed, and the carter came when he pleased. The ink never hardened, though she washed the slab at ten. The sun had not descended; the chimneys were still bright. The ledger's last page corrects a guess of mine: I had put the closing a year early. No date stands there to fix the order of anything. Her handwriting is not on it; a bindery clerk kept the book. It shows nothing of how the work was priced. It names no others who worked there, only herself.

She needed a lease at a fixed rent, and the landlord signed none. Someone to read her proofs aloud she never needed. The bench beside her held a second printer trained already. Work no copier could match kept arriving all that winter. Her storeroom stood above the water and her reams stayed dry.

My admiration for how she closed the shop carries one regret: she might have told us. Unreserved my admiration is not, whatever the ledgers show. Her silence draws no criticism from me; she owed us nothing. Detachment is beyond me; the shop was my own family's. Nor does her stubbornness amuse me.

options.F3P5-Q1-A: to fix the order in which events happened
options.F3P5-Q1-B: to name the others who worked there
options.F3P5-Q1-C: to correct a guess of the narrator's own
options.F3P5-Q1-D: to show how the work was priced

For fifty-eight autumns, volunteers at Culver Point have counted the hawks that cross the headland on their way south. They work from a wooden platform on the bluff, in four-hour shifts, tallying each bird by hand on a paper card. The resulting archive is one of the longest continuous records of raptor migration on this coast, and the Ridgeway Trust has used it to argue that three species are in decline.

In 2019 the Trust mounted an automated radar unit twenty metres from the platform. It was expected to confirm the hand counts. It did not. Across the first season the radar reported roughly a third more birds than the counters did, and the excess was not spread evenly: on cool September mornings the two records nearly matched, while on the warm afternoons late in the season the radar ran far ahead of the platform.

Neither instrument was obviously broken. Both had been serviced that summer; the volunteers were experienced, and several had counted for more than twenty years. The Trust spent two seasons on the question, pairing the two records hour by hour and sending an observer aloft in a light aircraft on eleven afternoons to see what each machine was seeing. The flights settled it. On warm afternoons the hawks climbed on warm air to eight hundred metres and beyond, where a bird is a speck or nothing at all to someone looking up from a bluff. The radar still registered them; the platform could not. The counters had never been counting the whole migration, only the part that passed low enough to see.

The Trust did not treat the archive as an error. It measures low passage faithfully, and it has measured the same thing for fifty-eight years. What changed was the label: the series is now published as a count of low-flying migrants rather than of migrants, and the decline it reports is a claim about that narrower quantity. The two instruments, the Trust concluded, answer two different questions.

options.F3P6-Q1-A: It is left untouched, while the radar is re-tuned and barred from publication until it can reproduce a season the volunteers already counted.
options.F3P6-Q1-B: It is published beside the radar series with its coverage described, and the Trust has declined to issue any combined total at all.
options.F3P6-Q1-C: It is being reprocessed under a correction factor fitted by hour of shift, which is expected to yield a shallower decline than the raw series.
options.F3P6-Q1-D: It is kept unchanged and republished under a narrower label, as a count of low-flying migrants rather than of migrants generally.
options.F3P6-Q1-E: It is closed rather than continued, since the rewritten counting rule restarts the trend from 2019 and cannot be joined to the old figures.

Ketch Bar is a low sand island off the eastern shore of Marrow Island, and for a century it held the largest breeding colony of ash-mantled noddies on this coast. Between one spring and the next, the birds stopped coming. Four explanations have been repeated ever since: a ground predator from the mainland, the wearing away of the bar, the traffic of the new ferry at Marrow Point, and the failure of the glass sprat, the small fish the noddies hunt. Okoye's team spent three seasons deciding among them.

The evidence supports the second. Stakes on the bar's crown show that it has lost most of its height, and storm water now crosses the whole flat. No rat has ever been taken here: two seasons of traps produced none, and the eggshell once reported as punctured was gull work. The ferry cannot account for the loss, since the crossings began four years after the last birds had gone. Nor did the sprat fail: the shoals offshore are as thick as ever, and noddies feeding there carry full loads to a colony farther south.

The ebb through the channel drew sand from the bar's northern face season after season. The current lured nothing to the place, lifted no sample from the ground, and settled no argument by reasoning; it carried the bar away, a little at each tide. The keeper's logbook from Marrow Light predates the decline. What it supplies is a date: the keeper set down the weather each evening, and his entries fix the night the northern face was cut open. He kept no tally of nests, named no fish, and reported no disturbance.

The ground is gone, and no work done on the bar can bring it back; what is left is to find the colony another island. Removing an animal newcomer would change nothing, since none was ever here; rescheduling human activity would help nothing, since none of it reaches them; and no recovery offshore is needed, because their food was never short. The case is persuasive but not yet closed, and further seasons of survey are wanted. The team has claimed no more than its measurements allow, nor has it stopped short of the question that matters.

The ice on Miller's Pond goes out about two weeks earlier than it did when the town began writing the date down in the 1840s. A survey team spent four springs on the water asking why. Road dust does no work on the sheet: the team painted test panels on the ice, dusting half and sweeping half clean, and both sets melted through on the same day. The new dam sends no warmth down: loggers above and below the inflow agreed within a tenth of a degree all spring, and the years the gates stood shut changed nothing. Cores cut through snow and ice show the cover not changed at all, in March or in the weeks after ice-out, and the deepest-drifted bays open with the bare ice. The spring winds have not shifted: the ridge gauges give the same March run as the oldest charts, and the calmest springs broke up no later than the windiest.

The thermometer records are the whole of the case: a century of morning readings taken in one shelter on the ridge. March has warmed steadily across that century, and the warmest Marches in the column stand beside the earliest ice-outs, year for year. Warm air works on a sheet from above all month, and the pond now loses in March what it used to lose in April.

Two weeks of open water in March is two weeks more sun in the pond, and the trout spawn earlier for it. On the morning the sheet broke this spring, the dial in the shelter registered nine degrees above freezing before eight. Nothing in the four seasons caught us off guard, and every question we raised now has its answer. The same work would settle any pond of this size, and the town's questions were fair, a pleasure to answer. The case on this pond is closed, and nothing in it remains open.

options.F3P8-Q1-B: the depth had swung with no pattern

Most mornings the sea off northern Chile sends a wall of grey up the flank of Cerro Pelado. Fishermen have called it the camanchaca for as long as anyone can remember: a fog thick enough to soak a shirt, thin enough to see the sun through. It carries no rain. The village of Aguada, four hundred meters below the ridge, receives less than fifteen millimeters of rain a year and has no river, so for a century its water arrived by truck. In 2019 a research station on the ridge strung forty nets of fine polypropylene mesh across the fog's path. Droplets caught in the mesh, ran down into gutters, and fell through a pipeline to the village tanks.

The station has weighed the catch every day since. The record shows a steady slide. In 2019 the array delivered about 6,900 liters on an average day; by 2025 the same forty nets delivered about 4,100, a loss of two liters in every five. The decline appeared in every month of the fog season, and no single year stands out as unusual — each simply came in below the one before it.

Rosa Iturra, who has run the station since it opened, is careful to say that six years is a short record. Still, she thinks the cause is legible. A warmer ocean surface has pushed the top of the fog layer upward, and the camanchaca now spends more hours drifting above the nets than through them; her instruments put the layer's base an average of thirty meters higher than in 2019. The comparison she trusts most is Cerro Bravo, a ridge twelve kilometers south whose nets sit three hundred meters higher. Cerro Bravo's yield has not fallen. The fog, she says, has not left; it has climbed.

What to do about it is a separate question. Iturra has asked the region for money to rebuild the array two hundred meters upslope, where the layer's new base sits, and the village council has voted to apply. She is blunt about what the move buys: nets on higher ground would return Aguada to its 2019 catch, but if the layer keeps rising at thirty meters every six years, the village will be climbing the ridge again within a generation. Aguada, she says, can stay ahead of the fog for a while — it cannot stay level with it.

options.F3P9-Q1-A: The prevailing wind has swung, so winter fog now slides past the ridge's shoulder while summer fog meets the array head-on.
options.F3P9-Q1-B: The crew's early improvements are exhausted, so the nets now take nearly all the water the passing fog will surrender.
options.F3P9-Q1-C: The ocean has warmed and lifted the fog layer, so the camanchaca now passes above the nets more often than through them.
options.F3P9-Q1-D: The eastern Pacific alternates warm and cold, so fog is abundant in warm-phase years and starved in cold-phase years.

When Ada Ferris ran the Whitlow schools cross-country course in nineteen minutes and four seconds, the time stood for a fortnight before the committee struck it out. Five reasons were argued at the hearing: a course measured short, a following wind along the ridge, a clock started late, a summer of hill training, and a route diverted around a flooded hollow that cut the last climb.

The hearing found the course short. A surveyor's wheel made it four hundred metres under, and the fault lay in one mismeasured boundary. The ridge gauge read calm, and no wind touched the field. One gun only was fired, and the clock started with it. Ferris trained on no hills that summer and raced unrested. No diversion was made; the hollow was dry and the climb run.

Her school beat Corran that afternoon, defeated them by two points. No pulse throbbed in her throat; she finished breathing easily. No rain struck the marquee, the afternoon staying dry. No path was tramped through the beech wood, which is fenced. The marshals searched no hedges, no boy having strayed. The flags along the ridge marked the halfway point for the runners. Slack on their poles, the flags showed no direction. No marshal was posted at the flags that afternoon. Plain white, they carried no school colours. The flags belong to no village custom, being bought that year.

Future records here will depend on a surveyed course, certified before the season opens. A wind reading at the ridge would record calm air. Two clocks would have shown what one clock showed. The present rules did not suffice on this occasion. A route fixed against alteration is what the field ran.

The committee's decision has my support, and I offer it without qualification. Their two-week delay earns no impatience from me. The decision strikes me as in no way harsh. Thoroughly astonished is how the decision leaves me. Nothing in the decision saddens me on Ferris's account.

options.F3P10-Q1-A: how a late clock produced a false time
options.F3P10-Q1-B: how a short course produced a false time

options.F3P10-Q1-D: how honest training produced a genuine time

For six years the nursery beds behind the Ferndale field station produced two very different crops of paper-bark hazel. Seedlings in the west beds grew fast and bushy; those in the east beds stayed short and thin. Staff had proposed four explanations, and each had its defenders: the west beds caught more afternoon sun; they had been dosed years earlier with mycorrhizal fungi; they were watered on a different schedule; and an old hedgerow sheltered them from the valley wind. Dr. Talia Renko argued that the four were not equally easy to check, and that one of them could be isolated in a single season. In April she chose that one.

Renko's target was the wind. She potted one hundred and twenty hazel seedlings in sterilized soil and split them into halves of sixty. Around each treatment pot she set a fine mesh screen that cut the valley gusts by about half; each comparison pot got a frame of the same size and the same position with the mesh left out of it, which threw the same thin shadow and left the moving air unchanged. Both halves received the same baked, fungus-free root dose, stood on one gravel bench in full sun, and drew from a single watering line.

Ten weeks later most of the measurements were dull. Root mass, stem height, and leaf count differed between the halves by less than four percent. Stem thickness did not: the treatment seedlings had stems twenty-four percent thicker than their counterparts. What Renko called the clearest sign, though, was not a number. Through the storm on the third of August, the treatment seedlings kept their new shoots, while the comparison seedlings lost theirs at the base.

Dr. Femi Aluko raised an objection Renko had not anticipated. The two halves had not gone into their pots at the same time: the treatment seedlings were potted in April and the ones she compared them with a month later, in May. Matching planting dates had not occurred to her. Matching ages had — every seedling came from one germination batch — and every pot held four liters, and a technician who did not know the groupings read every ruler. Renko granted the objection its force. Next April she will run the trial again with every seedling potted on a single day.

Until then, she says, the west beds keep their secret, and three of the four explanations stand untested.

options.F3P11-Q1-D: Through the storm on the third of August the treatment seedlings kept their new shoots, while the comparison seedlings lost theirs

Before the 1880s, each American town set its clocks by the sun. When the sun stood highest in the sky, it was noon. Because the sun appears to move from east to west, noon in Boston came about twelve minutes earlier than noon in New York.

For most people, this caused few problems. A farmer rarely traveled far enough in a day to notice. But the railroads changed that. A train crossing several states passed through dozens of local times, and each railroad printed its schedules using its own choice of clock. One station in Pittsburgh is said to have shown six different times. Travelers missed their connections, and trains sharing the same track risked crashing into each other.

In 1883, the railroads took matters into their own hands. They divided the country into four time zones, and on November 18, stations reset their clocks to match. Some towns grumbled about "railroad time" and kept the sun's time for a while. Yet within a few years, most of them had switched.

Congress did not make the zones official until 1918, thirty-five years after the railroads first used them.

options.F3P12-Q1-B: Time zones made the first railroads possible, since trains could not run safely until all the clocks in the country matched.
options.F3P12-Q1-C: Congress made time zones to bring order to the railroads, whose mixed-up times had confused travelers.
options.F3P12-Q1-D: Trains made each town's sun time hard to follow, so the railroads set up time zones that the nation later took up.

The landing at Vess was three planks and a post, and Oskar was already standing on it when Marta came down the hill. He did not greet her. He looked at the bundle under her arm the way he looked at weather, as a thing that would decide how the morning went.

Inside the oilcloth was a tin of seed rye, all that the flood had left dry on the home place. Her uncle held ground on the far side, high and stony and never once planted, and she was carrying the tin over to put it into that ground before the season closed.

"Sit forward," he said. "Boat's tender."

The water that morning was under fog, a low white one that took the shore away behind them before the boat had gone thirty yards and gave nothing at all ahead. There was no wind at all. Sounds arrived from directions that could not be right.

Marta had crossed this water twice before, both times as a child, and remembered nothing of it but the knock of the oarlocks. That knock was the same. Everything else had a size she had not expected.

Oskar rowed by count. He said the numbers under his breath, stopped at forty, held the oars up dripping and listened for the bell on the Vess side, and when he had it he turned the bow a little and started counting again.

"Nobody has ever had a crop off it," Marta said. "That is not the same thing as nothing will grow." She had been saying it to herself all week; out loud it sounded like somebody else's plan.

Fifty yards short of the piling the boat went soft on a sandbar and stopped. Oskar took the fare and shook his head at her look. "She will not float off with a load in her. It is shallow the whole way in."

Marta stepped out. Behind her the oarlocks started again, and she did not turn around to watch them go.

passage: Scientists once marked a small fish called a cleaner wrasse with a colored spot. After the fish saw itself in a mirror, it scraped its body against rocks. Some scientists said this proved the fish was self-aware, like apes and dolphins. We should be careful, though. Passing this mirror test may only show that an animal can link a reflection to its own body. That does not require any idea of a self. The wrasse's way of life gives a simpler answer. This fish gets its food by finding spots on other fish and picking them off. So it may be ready to react to a spot wherever it sees one, even in a mirror.

In 1849 the board of Hallowdean, a market town on the river Ledd, met to settle a six-year question: how to carry stone from the ridge quarries to the wharves. The board resolved upon a railway spur joining the town to the main line. Devitt's canal branch running down to the river wharves went down on the second reading.

Why the railway? Marrable told the board his furnaces would go elsewhere unless the work was begun, and the vote followed within a day. No covenant of repair binds Devitt or his heirs anywhere in the ledgers, which he kept himself. Thorne noted that the turnpike road carried across the high ridge was refused for want of a trust. The surveyors found the ground fit for every one of the four schemes. The quarrymen who petitioned for a horse tramway run down to the stone quarries went home empty. The roll of voting ratepayers was not enlarged in the eight years on either side of the vote.

Then came the check that Thorne recorded in his neat hand: a schedule of tolls so framed that the neighbouring carriers could not compete. No frost closed the work for a season, and the winter receipts never fall. The receipts of the first decade survive entire. The weighbridge returns were examined once a year at the audit, not weekly. Traffic rose steadily to the end of the decade. Numbered brass tokens belong to a later generation of gate practice, and none passed here.

One private source survives, the diary of Pell, the schoolmaster. Its worth is that it exposes an omission in the official record, the minute-book saying nothing of the members who withdrew. Pell was not present, and confirms no part of the account given in the official record. Foresight it did not show, the traffic never doubling as the members expected. The clerk entered the date twice, so the diary supplies none the official record leaves out. Circumstance did not force the choice so far that praise and blame are beside the point. Pell's memory has never been faulted, and his pages are no warning against trusting a private recollection. The board acted carelessly, and the praise later given it is not deserved. The mayfly hatch on Lake Ferrin once darkened the village streetlights for a week each June, and it has not done so since 2011. Five causes have been proposed: perch stocked for anglers, a dam trapping the silt the nymphs burrow in, fertilizer running off the lakeside farms, a raised weir drowning the shallows, and water warmer than before. Three summers of survey work point one way.

The surveys point to the dam. The silt the nymphs burrow in has not passed it since 2009, and the bed below is bare gravel. The stocked perch eat no nymphs, their stomachs holding snails. No algae bloom has formed; the farms' runoff stays low. The weir was never raised; its boards sit as in 1950. The lake runs no warmer than it did, June for June.

A spring feeds the north bay, a source of cold water all summer. Nothing climbs in that season; the shallows stay cold. The gauge holds no coil, working by float and chain. No trout leap for flies here, the lake having none. The trouble has no single origin anyone has found. The club's catch book dates the last big hatch to June of 2010. No change in the fishing appears there after the stocking. No members are named in it, only weights and dates. The catch book records no weather of any kind. No boast about the fishing is preserved there.

Return depends on passing silt below the dam, which a sluice could manage. Taking the perch out would gain nothing; the nymphs are safe from them. A buffer strip along the farms would catch runoff that never comes. Lowering the weir boards would uncover shallows never drowned. Cooler summers would help nothing, the lake being cool enough.

The club's conduct puzzles me; it paid for the survey and then ignored it. The club's conduct earns no praise from me. Its conduct rouses no anger in me. No hope comes to me from the club's conduct. Indifference is not what the club's conduct meets from me.

The grain hall at Ashbury was raised in 1729 and stood empty by 1848, its floor let out for hay. Five causes are named in the local histories: the mill's move upstream; the ending of the corn rent; the new canal to Marchford; the failure of the Ashbury bank; the fire of 1841. The parish records decide among them.

The mill did it. The mill went three miles upstream in 1836, and the carters followed it rather than turn back. Marchford's tolls never undercut Ashbury's, and the waggons kept coming. No fire touched the roof, whose trusses are the original oak. The corn rent ran on in kind until 1860, quite unchanged. The bank stood firm and trades today under the same name.

The charge of powder for the quarry was kept dry in the hall cellar. The porters took no fee, being paid by the vestry direct. Nobody was ever accused of anything within those walls. No bull ever rushed the market gate in living memory. The churchwarden had no duty there, the hall being the corporation's.

The churchwardens' book runs unbroken from 1701 to 1899. It supplies the carters: the new way past the upstream wheel is entered mile by mile. No tolls appear in it, Marchford's or Ashbury's. The August pages carry no fire and no loss of trusses. Payments in kind are absent from it altogether. No factor's dues are entered, and no page is ruled off.

Had the mill stayed at its old wheel, the hall would be trading yet; no other cause on that list emptied it, so no other rescue was possible. The credit here belongs to the churchwardens' book, and I give it gladly. The local histories are worth keeping, and I would throw none away. I offer the histories no correction on any single point. Nothing in them is comic, and the town believed them entirely. The vestry wrote down plenty, and I wish for nothing more.

For eleven days Ivo had been making a hare. It was to stand on the ridge of the Marchetti farmhouse: copper, hammered hollow, its ears set back as though it had just heard something move in the grass. On the twelfth morning he carried it up the stairs from the bench room, set it on Mrs. Hallam's table in the front shop, and put his hands behind his back so that she would not see them shaking.

She did not touch it at first. She walked around the table twice, the way she walked around a horse, and then she carried the hare to the window and held it up against the grey light of the yard. Petra, who had been four years with Mrs. Hallam and was allowed now to letter the invoices, went on ruling her lines and did not look up, which Ivo understood as a kindness.

"Here," she said at last, and turned the hare over so that the underside of the shoulder came into the light. The seam there was bright and a little beaded, run fast and hot in one pass. "You closed this in a single breath. It looks well this morning. It will look well next June. In the third winter the water will find the places where you did not wait for the metal to come up to you, and this shoulder will open like a seed pod."

Ivo asked whether he might carry it down again and open the seam and run it a second time, slowly, before it went anywhere. Mrs. Hallam said no. She wrapped the hare in sacking, wrote Marchetti, ridge, north face in the ledger, and stood it by the door for the carter, who came at ten. "It goes up as it is," she said. "The roof is a better teacher than I am, and it is slower, which is the whole of its advantage."

When she had gone out to the yard, Petra put down her pen. "She sent my first three up exactly as they were," she said. "Two came back inside four years. She knew which two, and she let the roofs tell me." Ivo went down to the bench room and opened the small book where he kept his measurements, and at the head of a clean page he wrote the day's date, and under it, Marchetti hare, shoulder seam; and then, lower down and in smaller letters, the date of the third winter from this one.

For three summers a crew from the Larkin Field Station camped at Muddy Fork Pond to explain one change in its golden shiners: the fish now spawn nearly three weeks earlier in spring than they once did. Records were thin: the cabin owners on the north shore photographed nothing, the hatchery that stocked the pond burned its paperwork, the graduate student of that decade left no notes, and the angling club never kept a logbook. The dates survive only in the field station's own automatic recorder, whose archive of the shallows through that decade still holds them.

The crew divided the shallow end into sixteen mesh pens and altered one condition in each group of four, leaving the rest of the pond untouched. Water reached the pens through an intake pipe, inside which a hard scale of lime had to be chipped out twice a summer.

A disease emptied the pond of bass a decade ago. Pens fenced against bass spawned eleven days ahead of pens the bass could enter, and their absence by itself moved the date. Pens warmed by a heater spawned on the ordinary schedule, so warmer water is not the trigger. Pens lit through cleared water spawned a little late, the opposite of what clarity predicts. Pens fed extra plankton spawned no earlier than untreated pens, which rules out an early bloom. Pens held at a steady depth kept the ordinary date, so the dam's release schedule explains nothing.

The crew expects the change to undo itself: bass are already working back up the inlet, and on their arrival the shiners should spawn late again. The crew will keep counting through the return of the bass, so the work at the pond is not finished. No second measurement is pending; the pens settled the cause, and the crew says so plainly. The crew had published nothing about the pond before, so no claim of its own is being withdrawn, and the same should be true of any pond that has lost its bass.
